conventions.convention: Finite product sigma-algebras are iterated recursively as ⊗_{i<1} A_i := A_0 and ⊗_{i<n+1} A_i := (⊗_{i<n} A_i) ⊗ A_n.
On the completed product, section measurability is only an almost-everywhere conclusion, not a pointwise-for-every-parameter conclusion.
On this page, 'conformal' means biholomorphic and orientation-preserving; complex conjugation is excluded.
The holomorphic principal logarithm on the slit plane is kept distinct from the pointwise principal value on the negative axis; branch-defined powers use the holomorphic branch.
The Poincare metric on the disc is normalized as ds_D = 2|dz|/(1-|z|^2).
Infinite-product convergence is tail-based and requires a nonzero tail limit; the published definition is for real sequences.
The order of an entire function is defined only for nonzero entire functions by default; constant nonzero functions have order 0 and the zero function is excluded unless stated otherwise.

load_bearing.statement:
Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure spaces. Then:

1. the set function $E \mapsto (\mu \times \nu)(E)$ of
   [[def-product-measure-on-sigma-finite-spaces]] is a measure on
   $\mathcal A \otimes \mathcal B$;
2. for measurable rectangles,
   $$(\mu \times \nu)(A \times B)=\mu(A)\nu(B);$$
3. the measure $\mu \times \nu$ is sigma-finite; and
4. it is the unique measure on $\mathcal A \otimes \mathcal B$ with the
   rectangle formula.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,
u)$ be sigma-finite measure spaces, and let $f : X 	imes Y 	o [0,\infty]$ be product-measurable. Then $x \mapsto \int_Y f_x\,d
u$ and $y \mapsto \int_X f^y\,d\mu$ are measurable, and

$$\int_{X 	imes Y} f\,d(\mu 	imes 
u) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d
uight)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\muight)d
u.$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $E \in \mathcal A \otimes \mathcal B$. Then

$$\int_X \nu(E_x)\,d\mu = \int_Y \mu(E^y)\,d\nu.$$

Let $f:\mathbb D\to\mathbb D$ be holomorphic and satisfy $f(0)=0$. Then

$$|f(z)|\le|z|\qquad(z\in\mathbb D),\qquad |f'(0)|\le1.$$

Moreover, if either $|f(z_0)|=|z_0|$ for some $z_0\in\mathbb D\setminus\{0\}$
or $|f'(0)|=1$, then

$$f(z)=e^{i\theta}z$$

for some real $\theta$; conversely every rotation $z\mapsto e^{i\theta}z$
satisfies equality in both conclusions.

A holomorphic map $f:\mathbb D\to\mathbb D$ is an automorphism of $\mathbb D$ if
and only if there exist $a\in\mathbb D$ and $\theta\in\mathbb R$ such that

$$f(z)=e^{i\theta}\varphi_a(z)=e^{i\theta}\frac{a-z}{1-\overline a\,z}\qquad(z\in\mathbb D).$$

Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb C$ be open, and let $(f_n)_{n\ge0}$ be holomorphic
functions on $\Omega$ whose product is normally convergent in the sense of
[[def-normal-convergence-of-holomorphic-products]]. Assume moreover that no
factor $f_n$ is identically zero on $\Omega$. Then the partial products

$$P_m(z):=\prod_{n=0}^{m}f_n(z)$$

converge locally uniformly on $\Omega$ to a holomorphic function $F$.

Moreover, on every compact set $K\subseteq\Omega$, all but finitely many factors
$f_n$ are zero-free and the tail limit is zero-free; therefore the zeros of $F$
on $K$, counted with multiplicity, are exactly those contributed by the finitely
many exceptional factors.

Let $f$ be an entire function, not identically zero. Let $m$ be the order of
its zero at $0$, and let $(a_n)_{n\ge1}$ list its nonzero zeros with
multiplicity and without finite accumulation point. Then there is an entire
function $g$ such that

$$f(z)=z^m e^{g(z)}\prod_{n\ge1}E_{p_n}(z/a_n)$$

for suitable integers $p_n\ge0$.

Let $f$ be a nonzero entire function of finite order $\rho$, let $m$ be the
order of its zero at $0$, let $(a_n)_{n\ge1}$ list its nonzero zeros with
multiplicity and without finite accumulation point, and put

$$p:=\lfloor\rho\rfloor.$$

Then there is a polynomial $Q$ of degree at most $p$ such that

$$f(z)=z^m e^{Q(z)}\prod_{n\ge1}E_p(z/a_n).$$

Let $f$ be holomorphic on a neighbourhood of the closed disc $\{|z|\le R\}$,
assume $f(0)\ne0$, and let $a_1,\dots,a_N$ be the zeros of $f$ in $|z|<R$,
counted with multiplicity. If $f$ has no zero on $|z|=R$, then

$$\log|f(0)|=\frac{1}{2\pi}\int_0^{2\pi}\log|f(Re^{it})|\,dt-\sum_{k=1}^{N}\log\frac{R}{|a_k|}.$$

Let $f$ be a nonzero entire function of finite order $\rho$, and let
$(a_n)_{n\ge1}$ list its nonzero zeros with multiplicity and without finite
accumulation point. Then the exponent of convergence of $(a_n)$ satisfies

$$\lambda\le\rho.$$

published_dependencies.used_for: Choice hypothesis in the countable/cocountable-section counterexample and false statement.
Countability closure needed to show initial sections of countable ordinals are countable.
Monotone-class closure step in the section-measure and iterated-section arguments.
Passage from finite or truncated product data to full Tonelli/Fubini equalities.
Simple-function approximation in Tonelli, layer-cake, and change-of-variables proofs.
Uniqueness of product measure and identification with Euclidean Lebesgue measure.
Completion step in the Euclidean-product and change-of-variables arguments.
Representative-picking step in completed-product Tonelli/Fubini.
Transfer of integrals from base-measurable representatives to completed-product functions.
Almost-everywhere section measurability on completed products.
Borel generation background for the Euclidean product theorem.
Borel-product inclusion via coordinate projections and image/preimage control under diffeomorphisms.
Area/volume inputs for Cavalieri and polar-coordinate remarks.
Radius-scaling consequence referenced by the polar-coordinate remark.
Plane Gaussian evaluation in the one-dimensional Gaussian example and the polar-coordinate remark.
Explicit iterated-integral computation in the non-L1 Fubini counterexample.
Series expansion in the zeta(2) double-integral example.
Termwise summation in the zeta(2) example.
Base definition for conformal equivalence and for several biholomorphism constructions.
Orientation-preserving conformal convention via nonvanishing derivative of a biholomorphism.
Published principal-logarithm and principal-power conventions compared against the new branch-based ones.
Holomorphic principal branch used in sector, slit-plane, and principal-strip maps.
Branch-power algebra and comparison with real powers.
Upper-half-plane automorphism classification as real Möbius maps.
Holomorphicity/invertibility of Möbius maps used in the upper-half-plane theorem.
Schwarz lemma removable-extension step.
Rigidity in Schwarz lemma and growth control in Hadamard factorization.
Boundary control on auxiliary functions in Schwarz lemma.
Derivative formulas in Schwarz-Pick and elementary-factor estimates.
Branch discrepancy theorem and uniqueness of holomorphic logarithms.
Constancy of branch differences and connectedness arguments for holomorphic logarithms.
Continuity of branch differences and slit-plane logarithm arguments.
Holomorphicity and derivative convergence for normally convergent products.
Polynomial conclusion for the exponential factor in Hadamard factorization.
Taylor expansion input for the sine product and Basel example.
Zero divisor of sin(πz) in the sine product theorem.
Jensen formula on discs.
Zero-free quotient logarithm in Weierstrass factorization and Jensen’s formula.
Plane/disc simply connectedness input for logarithm existence.
Published tail-based product convention that the infinite-product page tries to adapt to complex factors.
Absolute-convergence criterion and several infinite-product counterexamples.
Harmonic-series divergence in the genus-zero false statement.

concerns.concern: The finite-recursion paragraph defines the cases i<1 and i<n+1 but never the empty product i<0, even though the library's zero-based i<n convention allows n=0.
Fact [A2] is false as written: for n=1 the listed intersections are R_1 and R_1^c, whose union is X×Y, not R_1. Step 2.1 relies on that disjointification.

The remark invokes the Caratheodory extension route without carrying the countable-choice hypothesis from the cited extension theorem, and the stated uniqueness-on-A⊗B conclusion is not supported by the two cited items alone.
Step 1.1 shows rectangles lie in C_m, but to use the monotone-class theorem with the rectangle algebra it still needs C_m to contain finite disjoint unions from that algebra.
The proof checks closure of D_{n,m} under increasing limits, but the monotone-class appeal also needs the decreasing-half closure or some other route to the full generated sigma-algebra.
Step 1.2 states a sequence E_1,E_2,... but defines F_N as a union over k≤N, which clashes with the library's zero-based indexing convention when N=0.

The last paragraph asserts agreement with the published pointwise principal power, but the cited dependencies here only fix the principal logarithm and the branch-power construction; the principal-power identification is uncited.
Step 3.1 uses step 2.1 as if the induction on nonnegative integers had already been discharged, but step 2.1 is only the inductive implication under the hypothesis in 1.2.
The title says branch powers differ by roots of unity, but for general complex α the factor e^{2πiαk} need not be a root of unity; taking α=i already gives e^{-2π}.

The 'Why the group operation is legitimate' paragraph never cites or proves that compositions of holomorphic maps are holomorphic, and it only explicitly checks holomorphy for f^{-1}∘g^{-1}, not for g∘f itself.
The paragraph concluding that the Blaschke factor is holomorphic on a neighbourhood uses quotient-closure facts that are not supplied by its sole cited dependency.
The remark says the published infinite-product definition is being reused for complex factors, but the opened published definition is explicitly for sequences of reals.
Step 3.1 needs a positive lower bound from the real product ∏(1-|a_n|), but fact [F2] as stated inside this item does not record the needed (1-p_n)-criterion from the published theorem.
Fact [F1] cites the normal-convergence theorem but drops its extra hypothesis that no factor is identically zero on Ω.
Step 1.1 differentiates through the expression 1+u+...+u^{p-1}; when p=0 that shorthand needs a separate empty-sum interpretation or a separate case.

The canonical genus is defined as the least integer p for which the fixed-genus canonical product converges, but some discrete zero sequences have no such finite p; the definition needs an infinity case or an existence restriction.
Step 2.1 uses the sharper estimate |1-E_p(z/a_n)|≤|z/a_n|^{p+1}, while fact [F1] inside the theorem records only the weaker constant-e bound.
